design_detail: Open-label randomized controlled trial (ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01103531) in a publicly funded residential treatment programme in Southern California, 2010 to 2013: 135 adults with methamphetamine dependence newly admitted to residential treatment were randomized (computerized urn randomization stratified by sex and severity of use) to a supervised progressive aerobic and resistance exercise programme or to an equal number of group health-education sessions. This report analyses weekly Beck Depression and Beck Anxiety Inventory totals over the programme with mixed-effects models. The same trial is reported elsewhere for methamphetamine use after discharge, fitness, heart-rate variability, dopamine receptors and craving.
can_establish: Whether, during residential treatment in early abstinence, people randomized to a supervised exercise programme reported larger falls in depression and anxiety scores over the programme than people randomized to health-education sessions.
cannot_establish: Whether exercise itself, rather than knowing one was in the exercise group, lowered self-rated symptoms (no blinding, self-report outcomes); whether effects last after the programme (follow-up data registered but not reported here); whether more exercise causes more benefit (attendance was not randomized); effects outside residential treatment, in people with major depression (excluded by the registry criteria), or in people who use methamphetamine occasionally.

sample.recruitment: Clients newly admitted to a publicly funded residential treatment programme (registry: Cri-Help, North Hollywood, California), recruited by flyers in the facility, 2010 to 2013.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Methamphetamine dependence, English proficiency, age 18 to 45 for men or 18 to 55 for women, able to attend sessions; excluded for medical impairment affecting safety, opiate dependence, or psychiatric impairment needing hospitalization or primary treatment (Procedures, 1st paragraph). The registry adds DSM-IV-TR dependence, normal vital signs and ECG, and exclusion of major depression, psychosis and bipolar illness, among others.
sample.demographics: Mean age 31.7 (SD 6.9), range 18 to 47; 29.6% women; 48.1% Latino, 41.5% non-Latino white, 4.4% African American, 3.7% Asian; 16.3% employed in the month before entry; 64.7% with high-school education; 15.9 (SD 9.9) days of methamphetamine use in the month before entry (Results › Participant characteristics).
sample.attrition: Two participants (one per group) discharged for positive drug tests and excluded from analyses. The number contributing data at the end of the programme is not given in the text (the CONSORT diagram is an image); the registry says early discharge from the facility ended study participation.
sample.selection_effects: Treatment-seeking adults in one residential programme who volunteered for an exercise trial and passed medical screening; people with major depression were excluded by the registry criteria, so the sample began with mostly minimal to mild depressive symptoms.

exposure.measurement: Randomized assignment; attendance recorded by sign-in sheets.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Study conditions: exercise three times a week for 8 weeks (24 sessions) of about 55 minutes (the abstract says 60): 5-minute warm-up, 30 minutes on a treadmill at 60% to 80% of maximum heart rate (registry: 60% to 85%), 15 minutes of weight training of the major muscle groups, 5-minute cool-down; individually supervised by an exercise physiologist, with progressive increases in treadmill speed or slope and in weights. Control: 24 group health-education sessions of 55 minutes on stress reduction, health screening, healthy relationships and sexually transmitted diseases (registry: also healthy eating, meditation, sleep hygiene, cancer screening). Participants received a $10 gift card per session attended. Questionnaires at baseline, weekly and at discharge (week 9). Attendance: exercise 17.4 (SD 7.3) sessions, health education 18.5 (SD 7.0).
exposure.polysubstance: People with opiate dependence were excluded; other substance use is not reported.
exposure.abstinence_at_testing: Abstinence required by the facility and checked by random urine screens at least weekly; a positive test led to discharge.

comparison.controls: Health-education sessions of equal number and length, in group format, within the same residential treatment.
comparison.matching: Randomization stratified by sex and by severity of use (18 or fewer against 19 or more days in the previous month). The text says groups did not differ at baseline, but the reported baseline anxiety means differ by 4.6 points (see reporting issues).
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: Not applicable to the randomized comparison; baseline imbalance in anxiety is relevant.
comparison.controls_other_drug_use: Same facility rules for both groups.

outcomes.instruments: Beck Depression Inventory (21 items, 0 to 63) and Beck Anxiety Inventory (21 items), self-completed at the end of each week; weekly totals analysed.
outcomes.validity_norms: Standard validated self-report scales; the paper gives the usual BDI bands (0 to 13 minimal, 14 to 19 mild, 20 to 28 moderate, 29 to 63 severe).
outcomes.operationalization: Change in weekly total scores over the programme (treatment by time interaction); secondary: a three-way interaction of sessions attended, group and time.
outcomes.multiplicity_correction: None (two primary outcomes in this report, plus attendance analyses).
outcomes.assessor_blinding: None: the registry records masking as none (open label); outcomes were self-reported by participants who knew their group.

analysis.effect_sizes: Mixed-effects repeated-measures models, adjusted for demographics. Depression: treatment by time beta -0.63, P = 0.001; at the end of the programme BDI 2.43 (SD 4.22) with exercise against 4.82 (SD 5.71) with health education. Anxiety: beta -0.95, P = 0.001; BAI 2.18 (SD 4.94) against 5.11 (SD 7.79). Editors' calculation from these figures, assuming all randomized participants contributed: differences of 2.4 and 2.9 points, standardized about 0.48 and 0.45. Attendance by group by time: depression beta -0.61 (95% CI printed as -0.20 to -1.02), P < 0.001; anxiety -0.22 (-0.42 to -0.06), P = 0.009. No confidence intervals are given for the main treatment by time effects.
analysis.covariates: Demographics (not specified); baseline score in the attendance models.
analysis.preregistration_detail: NCT01103531, first submitted 31 March 2010 at the start of the trial. Registered primary outcome: self-reported days of methamphetamine use over the 12 weeks after discharge. 'Psychiatric symptoms' is a registered secondary outcome, measured from baseline to discharge and to 12 and 26 weeks after discharge. This paper calls depression and anxiety its two primary outcomes and reports only the programme period.
analysis.selective_reporting: The post-discharge psychiatric-symptom data registered as part of the secondary outcome are not reported here; the attendance analyses are described as secondary and not pre-specified in the registry.
analysis.power: Planned for 130 participants to give 80% power to detect a 3.5-point difference (SD 5) from baseline to the end of the programme; the observed end-of-programme differences (2.4 and 2.9 points) are smaller than that target.

interpretation_gap.results_show: Both groups' depression and anxiety scores fell steeply during residential treatment (from mild or minimal levels to near zero); the exercise group ended about 2.4 BDI and 2.9 BAI points lower than the health-education group, with significant group by time interactions. The exercise group had started with higher anxiety.
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract concludes that results support a structured exercise programme "as an effective intervention" for depression and anxiety in methamphetamine abstinence, and the discussion recommends that providers encourage this kind of exercise. Gaps: (1) open-label allocation with self-reported outcomes cannot separate exercise from expectation and attention; (2) the larger fall in anxiety in a group that started 4.6 points higher is partly what regression to the mean would produce; (3) the end-of-programme differences are below the trial's own planned minimum difference; (4) the 'dose effect' rests on attendance, which participants chose; (5) the outcomes were secondary in the registry, with follow-up not reported.

timeline.event: Trial registered (NCT01103531); design paper Mooney et al. 2014 (Contemp Clin Trials 37:139-147).

This report (depression and anxiety); companion reports of the same trial: Haglund et al. 2015 (predictors of depression outcomes) and Rawson et al. 2015 (methamphetamine use after discharge, Drug Alcohol Depend 156:21-28).
Xu et al. systematic review lists this trial three times among 17 entries on exercise in methamphetamine use disorder.

replication.where_it_stands: The only randomized trial of exercise for depression and anxiety in early methamphetamine abstinence read here with numbers; other trials reported in the same direction (mostly in Chinese compulsory rehabilitation) are known only through a review without numbers (xu_2024).

funding.funder: National Institute on Drug Abuse grant R01 DA027633.
funding.affiliations_note: UCLA Integrated Substance Abuse Programs and UCLA exercise physiology (Dolezal, Cooper); the same group published several reports of this trial.

what_would_settle_it: A trial with blinded outcome assessment or objective outcomes, an attention-matched active control, analysis of the registered outcomes at the registered times including after discharge, baseline-adjusted comparisons, and a sample that includes people with clinically significant depression and people outside residential care.

domains.note: Computerized urn randomization held by a data management centre, so concealment is plausible; but baseline anxiety differed by 4.6 points (about 0.8 SD by the editors' calculation) despite the text's statement of no difference.
Open label; participants attended about three quarters of sessions in both arms; two randomized participants were excluded from analysis; the analysis set at the end of the programme is not reported.
Early discharge ended participation (registry) and the number with week-8 data is not given in the text; mixed models assume data missing at random.
Self-reported depression and anxiety by participants who knew whether they were exercising, in a trial that the exercise group may have expected to help.

Registered as a secondary outcome with longer follow-up; this report presents it as primary over the programme period only, with several analyses (interaction terms, end-of-programme means, attendance models).

risk_of_bias.reasoning: High because the outcomes are self-reports by unblinded participants; the baseline imbalance in anxiety, unreported attrition and the shift from a registered secondary outcome add further concerns. May be cited for the observed difference between groups over the programme, with these limits; not for a causal effect of exercise on mood, for durability, or for a dose-response relation.

key_findings.finding: 135 adults with methamphetamine dependence in residential treatment were randomized: 69 to exercise and 66 to health education; mean age 31.7 (SD 6.9), 29.6% women, 48.1% Latino; 15.9 (SD 9.9) days of methamphetamine use in the month before entry. Two participants (one per group) were discharged for positive drug tests and excluded.
key_findings.locator: Methods › Procedures, 2nd paragraph; Measures, 2nd paragraph; Results › Participant characteristics

key_findings.finding: Baseline scores as reported: Beck Depression Inventory 13.7 (SD 5.3) with exercise against 12.0 (SD 6.3), P = 0.21; Beck Anxiety Inventory 16.5 (SD 6.0) against 11.9 (SD 5.1), P = 0.08.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Editors' calculation from these means and SDs with 69 and 66 participants: anxiety t about 4.8, p < 0.0001 (standardized difference about 0.8); depression p about 0.09. See reporting issues.

key_findings.finding: Depression: significant treatment by time effect (beta -0.63, P = 0.001), with BDI at the end of the programme 2.43 (SD 4.22) in the exercise group against 4.82 (SD 5.71) in the health-education group, after adjustment for demographics.
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Difference 2.4 points; editors' standardized difference about 0.48 if all randomized participants contributed (week-8 numbers not reported).

key_findings.finding: Anxiety: significant treatment by time effect (beta -0.95, P = 0.001), with BAI at the end of the programme 2.18 (SD 4.94) against 5.11 (SD 7.79).
key_findings.locator: Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
key_findings.note: Difference 2.9 points; editors' standardized difference about 0.45.

key_findings.finding: Attendance did not differ between arms (17.4, SD 7.3, sessions with exercise against 18.5, SD 7.0, with health education); more sessions attended went with lower depression and anxiety in both arms, and more so in the exercise arm (attendance by group by time: depression beta -0.61, P < 0.001; anxiety beta -0.22, 95% CI -0.42 to -0.06, P = 0.009).
No harms or unintended effects occurred in either group during the trial.

The trial was powered for a 3.5-point difference (SD 5) between groups in depression and anxiety change; the authors' limitations are a residential treatment sample, self-report measures, stress content in the health-education sessions, and a mostly male sample (70%).

Registry record: primary outcome self-reported days of methamphetamine use over 12 weeks after discharge; secondary outcomes include psychiatric symptoms from baseline to discharge and at 12 and 26 weeks after discharge; masking none (open label); first submitted 31 March 2010.
key_findings.locator: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT01103531, Study Plan › Design Details; Primary and Secondary Outcome Measures; Study Record Dates

reporting_issues.issue: The reported baseline P values do not fit the reported means and SDs: anxiety 16.5 (6.0) against 11.9 (5.1) with 69 and 66 participants gives t about 4.8, p < 0.0001 (editors' calculation), not P = 0.08; depression 13.7 (5.3) against 12.0 (6.3) gives p about 0.09, not 0.21. The text states there were no significant baseline differences.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: The exercise group probably started with clearly higher anxiety, so part of its larger fall may be regression to the mean; the anxiety result should be read as adjusted at best for demographics, not for baseline.

reporting_issues.issue: The text gives P = 0.03 for the effect of sessions attended on depression; Table 1 gives P < 0.001 for the same coefficient (-0.52, -0.83 to -0.22).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Dose effect; Table 1
reporting_issues.consequence: One of the two values is wrong; the confidence interval fits the table's value.

reporting_issues.issue: Several Table 1 P values do not match their confidence intervals (editors' calculation from interval width): baseline anxiety 0.23 (0.03 to 0.39) implies p about 0.01, printed < .001; treatment on anxiety -6.51 (-9.93 to -3.07) implies p about 0.0002, printed 0.02; sessions attended on anxiety (-0.42 to -0.16) implies p < 0.0001, printed 0.01; and the depression interaction interval is printed with its bounds reversed (-0.20, -1.02).
reporting_issues.consequence: The table's statistics cannot be taken at face value; the direction of the effects is not in doubt.

reporting_issues.issue: Depression and anxiety are called the two primary outcomes, but the registry lists self-reported methamphetamine use after discharge as the primary outcome and psychiatric symptoms as a secondary outcome with follow-up to 26 weeks after discharge, which is not reported here.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Methods › Measures, 1st paragraph; registry record NCT01103531
reporting_issues.consequence: Outcome switching between registration and report; the durability of any mood benefit is unknown from this paper.

reporting_issues.issue: The end-of-programme means (2.43 and 4.82; 2.18 and 5.11) are introduced in wording that could be read as change scores from baseline; read against the baselines they must be end-of-programme scores. The number of participants contributing at that time is not given.
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Results › Changes in depression and anxiety symptoms, 1st paragraph
reporting_issues.consequence: Standardized differences can only be approximated (editors' calculation assumes everyone randomized contributed).

reporting_issues.issue: The abstract and Methods give different session lengths for the exercise programme (exposure field).
reporting_issues.page: PMC HTML, Abstract › Methods; Methods › Intervention Condition
reporting_issues.consequence: Minor; the Methods describe the session in detail.
